source_checks: Southern peri-urban objective access disadvantage coexists with relatively optimistic access perceptions.
Urban-center and western peri-urban measured accessibility are similar, with different perceptions.
Western residents report greater basic infrastructure improvement needs and greater pandemic-era use vulnerability associated with quality perceptions.

generation_prompt:
Create a NEW sophisticated scientific graphical abstract, English only, for Wu et al. (2025), Landscape and Urban Planning: urban and peri-urban park equity during COVID-19 in Salt Lake City. This replaces a previous text-heavy comparison slide. The result must communicate through compact purposeful illustrations, not paragraphs or a large study-area map.

Canvas: approximately 4:3 landscape, opaque white. Refined contemporary scientific editorial illustration, crisp fine charcoal linework, controlled teal for objective measurements and muted vermilion for resident experience. A restrained urban-geography aesthetic, no watercolor or glossy 3D rendering. Use readable modest typography, all text horizontally set, balanced margins. Main illustrations take about 55% of canvas; the title about 10%. No invented empirical maps, charts, axes, scores or statistics.

Exact title: "Park equity beyond provision"
Small context line: "Salt Lake City · Urban and peri-urban communities"

Two adjacent unframed case compositions form the main graphic, with an open central gap and consistent alignment. This is one integrated figure. Do not surround cases with rounded cards. NO big background map and NO duplicated suburban house models.

LEFT CASE heading "SOUTHERN PERI-URBAN"
Make a compact, flat analytical illustration of two different assessment lenses:
Objective lens: a simple abstract spatial-network motif with one park symbol and a dashed accessibility boundary. No house-to-park user trace, no respondent locations, no real geography, no number of minutes or meters. This motif represents conventional spatial access measurement, not a measured map.
Resident lens: a separate clean survey-and-perception motif with a small speech shape and a stylized open park entrance. Do not connect a person to a particular park. The two lenses are slightly offset within the case to visibly express diverging assessments, without causal arrows.
Exact short labels near their respective motifs:
"Measured access disadvantage" in teal
"More optimistic perceived access" in vermilion
Small nearby connector label "Assessment mismatch".
Keep illustrations compact; the comparison itself is the focal point, not park scenery.

RIGHT CASE heading "WESTERN PERI-URBAN"
Make another compact analytical illustration: two simple distance/access measurement motifs, one labelled "Urban center", one labelled "Western peri-urban", visibly comparable and joined by a small open bracket labelled "Similar measured access". These are symbolic access-only comparisons, NOT identical park-quality scenes and NOT quantitative charts.
Below, an open small branch with two purposeful line illustrations representing resident-reported concerns: a bench-and-bin maintenance-request motif, and a park gate with a minimal COVID-era context marker. Label these respectively:
"Greater infrastructure needs"
"Use sensitive to quality perceptions"
Above this small pair, a concise label "Resident experience during COVID-19".
Use vermilion to highlight reported needs, not to imply measured severity. Do not show destroyed parks, closed gates, declining use graphs or virus causing disrepair. These illustrations represent categories of findings, not observations of particular facilities.
Connect the access comparison with the experience cluster using a subtle bracket for joint comparison, NEVER a causal arrow.

BOTTOM:
One concise scholarly takeaway, prominent but not huge:
"Resource measures can miss context-specific disadvantage."
A small framework line beneath:
"Compare access, quality, perceptions, needs and use."
Source footer:
"Wu et al. (2025) · Landscape and Urban Planning"
"Conceptual synthesis · Illustrations are schematic"

Factual invariants: The southern peri-urban group is disadvantaged by conventional spatial accessibility measures but has more optimistic perceptions than these suggest. Western peri-urban and urban-center groups have similar objective access but different perceptions; western communities report greater essential infrastructure needs and their pandemic-era park use is more vulnerable to quality perception issues. All diagrams illustrate regional assessments and are not directly linked individual-to-park data. Do not imply uniform peri-urban disadvantage, establish causality, claim a measured decline in use, or invent exact rankings, values, boundaries or survey distributions.

Composition goal: immediately see two DIFFERENT ways that resource-only evaluation can be incomplete. Each compact illustration must clarify its nearby finding. No giant repeated slogans, no ornamental skyline, no icon wallpaper, no wall of prose, no oversized empty panels. Diagram connectors indicate comparison/grouping only. Prefer sophisticated clear pictorial linework with small flat color accents, suitable for a top urban-geography or planning journal graphical abstract. Keep total text exactly limited to the specified labels, give findings enough space to read comfortably.
correction_prompt: Edit this graphical abstract with ONLY two changes. In the WESTERN PERI-URBAN lower-right illustration, swing both park gate leaves wide OPEN and leave a clearly unobstructed path; retain the resident and pandemic context. Under the bracket labelled 'Similar measured access', add a compact second line exactly 'Different resident perceptions'. Preserve all other words, scientific group assignments, illustrations, colors, white background, composition, and source footer. No causal arrows, no new maps or numbers. The gate must look open, not closed.
qa: Open park entrance avoids implying park closure.
Added different resident perceptions to the western comparison.
Regional schematics have no empirical coordinates, scales or causal arrows.
